introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections » ; `regles_choix` porte une règle `parmi 1 sur 3` par section (SECTION A, B, C, D), ce qui reproduit exactement la consigne (4 questions en tout, une par section). Les trois questions de chaque section sont numérotées de façon continue (1 à 12) dans le sujet.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « (25 marks) » et la couverture dit « All questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice vaut « 25 » et la question unique « 1 » porte 25. Aucun écart avec les points imprimés (4 x 25 = 100).

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde puis les douze questions), filigrane gcerevision.com en travers du texte sans incidence sur la lisibilité ; aucune figure, carte ni document. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 3 - Africa and World History, code 0760, JUNE 2020.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les dates, noms et traités sont ceux de l'historiographie établie ; les faits dont la précision est moindre sont formulés prudemment (pas de chiffre exact de victimes ni de résultats électoraux au-delà d'ordres de grandeur).

Question 4 : l'ordre précis des ralliements de l'Afrique équatoriale française en août 1940 (Tchad le 26, Cameroun le 27, Congo les 28-29) n'est pas détaillé dans le corrigé ; seul le mois est donné. Les effectifs d'Africains mobilisés sont dits « hundreds of thousands » sans chiffre.

Question 5 : la formulation du sujet (« more visible in the economic domain ») appelle une évaluation nuancée ; la participation exacte des compagnies françaises aux mines de Gabon (COMUF, COMILOG) et de l'ex-Elf à la production pétrolière est donnée dans ses grandes lignes sans pourcentage ni date de création précise.

Question 12 : le sujet dit « since 1948 » ; le corrigé mentionne les accords d'Abraham de 2020 (signés en septembre 2020, soit après la session de juin 2020 de l'épreuve) comme fait historique postérieur au sujet, ce qui n'a aucun effet sur la question posée.

questions.enonce_markdown:
For what reasons and with what consequences was the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade abolished in the 19th century?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade carried millions of Africans to the Americas from the 16th century. Britain, the leading carrier in the 18th century, made the trade illegal for its subjects in 1807 and slavery itself in its empire in 1833 (in force from 1834). Other powers followed more slowly, and illegal slaving continued for decades. The abolition was the result of a combination of humanitarian, economic and political causes, and it had far-reaching consequences for Africa, Europe and the Americas.

**1. Reasons for abolition**

*a) Humanitarian and religious reasons.* From the late 18th century, Quakers, Evangelical Christians and Enlightenment thinkers condemned the trade as contrary to Christian teaching and to the "rights of man". The Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade (1787) brought together Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce, who led the parliamentary campaign. Public opinion was moved by the testimony of former slaves such as Olaudah Equiano, by pamphlets, petitions and boycotts of slave-grown sugar, and by scandals such as the *Zong* case of 1781, when over a hundred enslaved Africans were thrown overboard from a British ship. The judgement in the Somerset case (1772) had already shown that slavery had no basis in English common law on English soil.

*b) Economic reasons.* Historians such as Eric Williams (*Capitalism and Slavery*, 1944) argued that by the early 19th century the West Indian sugar economy was in relative decline, while the Industrial Revolution created a new class of manufacturers and merchants who favoured free trade, wage labour and new markets rather than slave-based plantations. Africa was increasingly seen as a source of raw materials (palm oil, groundnuts, timber) and as a market for manufactured goods, a trade that could not flourish while Africans were being exported as slaves. This thesis is debated (other historians stress that the trade was still profitable in 1807 and that moral pressure was decisive), but the shift in economic interests clearly helped the abolitionists.

*c) Political reasons and resistance.* Slave resistance, culminating in the Haitian Revolution (from 1791, independence in 1804), frightened planters and showed that slavery could be overthrown. The French Revolution and the American Revolution spread ideas of liberty and equality. Britain, which dominated the seas after the Napoleonic Wars, also had the means and the interest to impose abolition on others, and the abolition of the trade became a matter of national moral prestige.

**2. How abolition was enforced.** Denmark decreed an end to its trade in 1792 (effective 1803), Britain passed the Slave Trade Act in 1807, and the United States banned the importation of slaves from 1808. The Congress of Vienna (1815) condemned the trade. Britain created the West Africa Squadron (1808) to intercept slave ships and signed anti-slavery treaties with European states and African rulers. Slavery itself was abolished in the British Empire by the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 (with compensation to owners), in the French colonies in 1848, and later in Cuba (1886) and Brazil (1888).

**3. Consequences**

*a) For Africa.* (i) The era of "legitimate commerce" began: exports of palm oil, palm kernels, groundnuts and later cocoa and cotton replaced slaves, benefiting new coastal middlemen and some states, but ruining others whose power depended on the slave trade (for example, the decline of Oyo and the readjustment of Dahomey). (ii) Settlements for freed slaves were founded: Freetown in Sierra Leone (1787, a Crown colony from 1808) and Liberia (1822, independent in 1847). (iii) Slavery inside Africa did not disappear; with more slaves kept at home to produce palm oil and other goods, domestic slavery often increased, and the trade in slaves from East Africa to the Indian Ocean continued. (iv) Christian missionaries, explorers and traders moved into the interior, and the need to protect "legitimate commerce" and suppress the trade was used by Europeans to justify intervention, treaties and, later, colonisation (for example the annexation of Lagos in 1861).

*b) For Europe and the Americas.* Britain gained prestige and a humanitarian image and strengthened its naval and commercial supremacy. In the Americas, illegal slave imports to Brazil and Cuba continued until the mid-century, and slave labour was progressively replaced by wage labour and indentured labour. Freed slaves in the Caribbean faced the "apprenticeship" system (to 1838) and economic hardship.

**Conclusion.** The abolition of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade resulted from a convergence of humanitarian campaigns, changing economic interests and political upheaval, none of which alone explains it. It ended the legal export of Africans, but it also reshaped African economies and opened the way to missionary activity and, eventually, European colonial rule.
